source.title: Double-descent curves in neural networks: a new perspective using Gaussian processes
source.authors: Ouns El Harzli; Bernardo Cuenca Grau; Guillermo Valle Pérez; A. Louis

record.file_problem: None apparent; the paper text includes the main sections and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: It analytically studies and simulates width-dependent NNGP kernel and GP regression using a different method from empirical sweeps of trained deep networks, and reports double descent in generalization error as the width-to-data ratio varies.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports spectral-distribution and kernel-value results, but these do not directly measure generalization error. They are not separate rows here. The double-descent curves and their stated outcomes are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study derives, and simulates, the generalisation error of width-dependent NNGP kernel and GP regression as the width-to-data ratio γ=n/N varies. It finds divergence at γ=1 and a finite error as γ→0. This is a non-deep-network model class (random last-layer features with an infinite-width NNGP backbone), so it bears on V4. It does not bear on V1, which concerns trained deep networks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors derive analytic generalisation error for kernel and GP regression with a width-dependent NNGP kernel, where only the last layer is finite. They predict double descent as last-layer width varies relative to sample count, attributing it to the discrepancy between the empirical and NNGP kernel spectra. They caution that quantitative accuracy depends on spectral universality, and that the theory covers only fully connected networks in infinite-dimensional limits.
record.recipe_differences: Uses random-matrix analysis of width-dependent NNGP kernels and GP/kernel regression, plus simulations; it does not reproduce empirical training and evaluation of the original deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different degrees of quantitative agreement across settings: very good agreement for isotropic data without nonlinearity, and acceptable but imperfect agreement for MNIST with ReLU. Generalization-error estimation relies on the spectral universality assumption.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors interpret double descent as governed by the spectral perturbation of the width-dependent empirical kernel relative to the NNGP kernel. That perturbation vanishes as γ→0, and eigenvalues near zero at γ=1 cause the divergence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In NNGP-derived regressions, double descent is driven by the spectral discrepancy between finite-width empirical kernels and the infinite-width NNGP kernel.

record.problems: The theory assumes infinite-dimensional limits and applies to fully connected architectures. Generalization-error estimates rely on spectral universality, whose validity may be incomplete for real-world data. The MNIST analysis uses a restricted subset and the authors report imperfect quantitative agreement there. Numerical curve values and uncertainty estimates are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Spectral-distribution comparisons (Figures 1 and 3) and kernel-value distributions (Figures 4 and 5) were not recorded as rows because they do not directly measure generalization error or another named version of the claim.

untested.parts: No trained finite deep networks; only last-layer width varies, with earlier layers infinite and no training (kernel/GP regression on random features).
No sweep of sample count at fixed width; γ and ψ are varied as ratios.
No single complexity measure predicting peaks across axes.
Label noise not varied. Peak shown only in the ridgeless limit; the claim that regularisation reduces the divergence is asserted, not measured. No multiple peaks.
Whether the overparameterised limit beats the underparameterised optimum is not stated; only finiteness of the limit is shown.

record.verdict_notes: V1 links were dropped because nothing is trained and only last-layer random features vary. Neither original source is this study. The peak is an infinite divergence that exists only in the noise-free (ridgeless) limit; the authors say regularisation reduces it but give no numbers, so this is not counted as a V6 test.

versions.untested_parts: The analysis concerns NNGP-derived kernel and GP regression, with width dependence in the last layer; it does not test ordinary training of finite deep networks or sweeps of widths across all layers.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
The study varies the asymptotic ratio γ=n/N, rather than isolating an increase in sample count at fixed model width.
Evidence is for the studied NNGP-derived kernel and GP regression settings, not a broad survey of model classes.
The paper proposes a spectral-discrepancy interpretation, but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
No controlled label-noise or variance sweep, multiple-peak test, or test of optimally tuned regularization eliminating the peak.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective parameter measure or test of whether that turns the curve into an ordinary U shape.

rows.subject: NNGP kernel regression with width-dependent kernel K^N
rows.operation_detail: Derives the limiting generalization error as γ varies with ψ fixed, in the noise-free limit.
rows.value: The paper states that the error exhibits double descent: it diverges as γ approaches 1 from either side, has an underparameterized asymptote as γ→∞, and a finite overparameterized limit as γ→0.
rows.note: The study describes γ=n/N as the ratio governing the width-dependent kernel regression curve.
rows.check: Subject is random-feature kernel regression (only the last layer is finite, nothing is trained), not a deep network, so the V1 link is removed. The result is an analytic derivation in the ridgeless limit σϵ→0; the peak is an infinite divergence at γ=1.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3, Corollary 1, equations (19)–(20) and following overparameterized-limit expression; lines 555–600.

rows.subject: Gaussian process regression with GP prior z_K^N
rows.operation_detail: Derives the limiting GP-regression generalization error as γ varies with ψ fixed, in the noise-free limit.
rows.value: The paper states that the same double-descent asymptotes hold for E_GP: divergence at γ→1 from either side and a finite overparameterized limit as γ→0.
rows.note: The corollary explicitly extends the result to GP regression.
rows.check: Same as R1: GP regression with a width-dependent random kernel, not a trained deep network, so V1 is removed. It is an analytic noise-free limit.
